name: Enteric Anendocrinosis
aliases: Congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea due to enteroendocrine cell dysgenesis

clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in NEUROG3 (neurogenin-3), the master transcription factor required for the specification of enteroendocrine cells along the gut.
Affected infants present with severe, life-threatening congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea that persists despite bowel rest, reflecting a generalised absence of intestinal hormone-producing cells.

The intestinal mucosa has normal villous architecture on light microscopy, but immunostaining reveals a striking paucity or absence of enteroendocrine cells (chromogranin A negative), which is the diagnostic hallmark.

Because so many gut peptides are lost simultaneously (cholecystokinin, secretin, GIP, GLP, motilin, somatostatin and others), the malabsorption is broad and refractory rather than confined to one nutrient.

Many patients later develop diabetes mellitus because the same transcription factor is required for pancreatic islet endocrine cell development, so the disorder bridges gut and pancreatic endocrinopathy.

It must be distinguished from other congenital diarrhoeas such as microvillous inclusion disease (MYO5B) and tufting enteropathy (EPCAM), which show characteristic epithelial architectural abnormalities that enteric anendocrinosis lacks.
Long-term survival usually depends on parenteral nutrition; the enteric endocrine defect itself is not correctable, so management is supportive.
The severity of diabetes and the age of onset vary with the residual function of the NEUROG3 variant, with hypomorphic alleles sometimes giving a milder or later phenotype.
reference.pathophysiology: Enteric anendocrinosis is an autosomal recessive congenital diarrhoeal disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in NEUROG3, the gene encoding neurogenin-3, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that acts as the obligatory master regulator for commitment of intestinal and pancreatic progenitor cells to the endocrine lineage. In the gut, neurogenin-3 is required for the differentiation of the full complement of enteroendocrine cells that secrete the peptide hormones coordinating digestion, motility, and nutrient sensing. When the factor is absent or non-functional, these cells fail to form, so the intestine is left essentially devoid of hormone-producing cells despite otherwise normal villous and crypt architecture; the resulting deficiency of gut peptides produces profound congenital malabsorptive and secretory diarrhoea from the first days of life. Because the same transcription factor is indispensable for the development of the endocrine pancreas, complete loss also impairs formation of the insulin-secreting beta cells and other islet cells, so many patients develop diabetes mellitus, often in infancy or childhood, giving a combined intestinal and pancreatic endocrine phenotype. The clinical severity broadly tracks the residual activity of the variant, with null alleles producing the most severe neonatal disease and hypomorphic alleles a comparatively attenuated course.
additionalDifferentials: Microvillous inclusion disease (MYO5B) — congenital secretory diarrhoea with abnormal apical enterocyte structure
Congenital chloride diarrhoea (SLC26A3) and congenital sodium diarrhoea
Glucose-galactose malabsorption and other congenital carbohydrate transport defects
Proprotein convertase 1/3 (PCSK1) deficiency causing malabsorptive diarrhoea with endocrinopathy
additionalInvestigations: Small bowel biopsy with chromogranin A and other enteroendocrine immunostaining showing absent or markedly reduced endocrine cells
Light microscopy of intestinal mucosa confirming preserved villous architecture
Stool electrolyte and osmotic gap analysis to characterise the diarrhoea
Fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin and pancreatic islet function testing given the diabetes risk
Nutritional and fat-soluble vitamin assessment during parenteral nutrition
Exclusion panel for other monogenic congenital diarrhoeas (MYO5B, EPCAM, SLC26A3, FOXP3)
redFlags: Severe watery diarrhoea from birth that fails to settle with bowel rest, indicating a congenital rather than infective cause
Rapid dehydration and electrolyte derangement in a neonate with high-output stool losses
Development of hyperglycaemia or diabetes in an infant with congenital diarrhoea
Failure to thrive and parenteral-nutrition dependence with associated line complications
Family history of consanguinity or affected siblings with congenital diarrhoea
reference.prognosis: The intestinal endocrine defect is permanent and most children remain dependent on parenteral nutrition, so prognosis is guarded and shaped by nutrition-related complications and the later emergence of diabetes. Outcomes are better with early diagnosis, meticulous nutritional support, and anticipatory management of the evolving endocrinopathy.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the illness as intractable infective or allergic diarrhoea and delaying genetic and immunohistochemical evaluation
Being reassured by normal villous architecture on routine histology without performing enteroendocrine immunostaining
Overlooking the pancreatic endocrine component and missing evolving diabetes
Confusing it with microvillous inclusion disease or tufting enteropathy, which have distinct epithelial features
Attempting escalating enteral feeds when the malabsorption is fundamentally hormone-deficiency driven
references: Clinical reference on congenital diarrhoeal disorders
Reference on monogenic disorders of endocrine development
management: Lifelong parenteral nutrition is the mainstay to sustain growth in the face of refractory congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea
Provide meticulous fluid and electrolyte replacement to correct the losses of severe malabsorptive diarrhoea
Supplement fat-soluble vitamins and micronutrients with regular nutritional monitoring
Prevent and manage parenteral-nutrition complications, including catheter-related sepsis and intestinal-failure-associated liver disease
Screen for and treat the later-developing diabetes mellitus with insulin, reflecting the shared pancreatic islet defect
Manage within a paediatric intestinal-failure, gastroenterology and endocrinology multidisciplinary team, considering intestinal transplantation in intractable intestinal failure
Confirm the diagnosis with NEUROG3 testing and provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder
